source: Ferreira, Wobbe, Krishnakumar, Hutter, Zela (2026) Can LLMs Beat Classical Hyperparameter Optimization Algorithms? A Study on autoresearch
finding: Independent group (AutoML) tested 9 HPO methods (4 classical, 4 LLM, 1 hybrid) on one 24-hour GPU budget. In a fixed search space, classical CMA-ES and TPE beat LLM agents. Letting the LLM edit code narrows but does not close the gap, even with Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview.
numbers: 14 hyperparameters, 3 seeds, val_bpb (lower better). Best means: Centaur 0.9763, TPE 0.9768, SMAC 0.9778, CMA-ES 0.9785, Karpathy Agent (Code) 0.9814; default 0.991. OOM rates: top methods at or below 16%, bottom four above 36%; LLAMBO 48% and 61%.
quote: classical methods such as CMA-ES and TPE consistently outperform LLM-based agents
limits: Small absolute gaps (0.0005 between top two). One task (small LM training), 3 seeds. Fixed compute budget, LLM inference cost excluded from wall time.
agent_relevance: Direct answer to gap 2: with a strong, independently run classical baseline the LLM loses as a standalone searcher. LLMs lose track of optimisation state. Use code-held state for the search and the LLM for proposals.

source: Ferreira et al. (2026) Centaur hybrid and LLM ratio ablation (same paper)
finding: Centaur shares CMA-ES state (mean, step size, covariance) with an LLM that proposes a fraction of trials. It gave the best result, and a 0.8B model already beat all classical and pure-LLM methods. Too many LLM trials hurts.
numbers: Centaur 0.8B r=0.1 gives 0.9744, r=0.3 gives 0.9766, r=0.8 gives 0.9849. Centaur 27B r=0.5 gives 0.9746, r=0.8 collapses to 0.9902. Best single seed 0.9741 (Centaur), worst 0.9829. Opus 4.6 Centaur 0.9739. Unconstrained code edit with 0.8B model 0.9910 vs 27B 0.9814; fixed-HP agent shows no gain from scale (0.9904 vs 0.9908).
limits: Same single task and 3 seeds. LLM ratio r was tuned on the same benchmark.
agent_relevance: Supports a gated design: code computes and tracks state, LLM proposes in a minority of steps (10-50%), and a state channel is shared with it. Supports K12 and gives a number for how much LLM share is useful.

source: Ferreira et al. (2026) diversity and domain-knowledge findings (same paper)
finding: Search diversity did not predict quality: avoiding out-of-memory failures mattered more. The single-agent LLM had the lowest diversity and converged to a narrow region early. LLAMBO was among the most diverse yet lost because of failures. CMA-ES lacked domain knowledge that the LLM supplied (for example an attention-pattern override).
numbers: Karpathy Agent (14 HPs) lowest diversity on all metrics; LLAMBO (Paper) among most diverse, 48% OOM, underperforms classical. Overrides listed in appendix A.6 where CMA-ES has no domain prior.
limits: Diversity here is over hyperparameter configs, not a Pareto front.
agent_relevance: Partly answers gap 9 and gap 3: diversity alone is not the bottleneck, feasibility is; LLM value is domain priors, not search mechanics.

source: Zhang, Desai, Bae, Lorraine, Ba (2024) Using Large Language Models for Hyperparameter Optimization
finding: Earlier positive result with older models: at 10 evaluations on 32 tasks (8 datasets x 4 search spaces) GPT-4 Turbo beat random search more often than BO.
numbers: Versus random search: GPT-4 Turbo 81.25% wins, median change 13.70%, mean 19.83%, mean rank 2.42; the other rows (GPT-4, GPT-3.5 Turbo, BO-RF, BO-GP; labels partly garbled in extraction) have ranks 3.48, 3.84, 3.45, 3.80. Random rank 4.00. Budget 10 evaluations.
limits: Row labels in the extracted table are partly garbled, so mapping of ranks to names is approximate except GPT-4 Turbo. Contamination not tested. Opposite in direction to d01 at larger budget with tuned classical methods.
agent_relevance: Shows the low-budget gain is real vs random and default BO at 10 evaluations, and it shrinks or reverses vs tuned classical methods at larger budget. Budget is the boundary condition.

source: Zhang, Liu, Lin, Wang, Lu, Zhang (2024) Understanding the Importance of Evolutionary Search in Automated Heuristic Design with LLMs (PPSN)
finding: Large benchmark of FunSearch, EoH, ReEvo and a plain (1+1)-EPS baseline on 4 heuristic design problems, 5 runs each. No LLM-search method wins everywhere. The simple (1+1) baseline is competitive except on online bin packing (Weibull). Standalone LLMs without search are not enough.
numbers: Budget 10,000 function evaluations, 5 independent runs, up to 9 LLMs (7 for the baseline comparison), 4 problems. EoH best on TSP. Authors state none of the EPS methods shows a clear advantage over standalone LLM on specific tasks at 10,000 queries; EPS beats standalone on AS, OBP (Weibull) and TSP but not OBP (OR).
limits: Small open models (CodeLlama, DeepSeek-Coder) plus some GPT-class; not frontier reasoning models. EoH authors are co-authors, but the paper is built as a neutral benchmark.
agent_relevance: Evidence for gap 2 and 10: weak baselines were common, and a simple elitist loop is hard to beat. Start the S7 loop simple and add structure only if it measurably wins.

source: Huang, Ye, Shahane, Back, van Stein (2026) From Heuristic Selection to Automated Algorithm Design: LLMs Benefit from Strong Priors
finding: Token attribution shows the example code and its strategy text in the prompt influence LLM-written algorithms most. Seeding a simple (1+1) elitist loop with existing benchmark algorithms (BAG) gives the best average rank in 5 of 6 benchmark-LLM settings against six LLM-driven methods. It cites Gideoni et al. 2025 (workshop): random baselines for simple code problems are competitive with code evolution (that cited paper not opened).
numbers: 3 LLMs (Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite, GPT-5 Nano, Qwen3 Coder Flash), 2 suites (pbo, bbob). With GPT and Qwen on bbob it improves mean normalised AUC over the strongest baseline by 23% and 22%; with Gemini within 1% of LLaMEA. On pbo with GPT it ranks second, -0.65% AUC vs EoH. One LLM query per candidate vs five for EoH.
limits: Small cheap LLMs. Gideoni et al. is cited, not opened.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 3: priors from known good algorithms (rules and exemplars) carry much of the gain, and a simple loop with them beats complex search. A rules-only (no LLM) baseline is still untested.

source: Sun, Feng, Li, Yang (2025) CO-Bench: Benchmarking Language Model Agents in Algorithm Search for Combinatorial Optimization
finding: 36 real combinatorial optimisation problems. One-shot LLMs score far below a classical solver, and reasoning models do better than non-reasoning ones. Agent search frameworks lift scores a lot. FunSearch (o3-mini based) tops the list and beats the classical solver. Some complex agents (AIDE) lose to simple BestOfN.
numbers: Classical solver avg score 0.797, valid 0.611. Best one-shot LLM Claude-3.7 Sonnet 0.65; o3-mini-medium 0.615; DeepSeek-R1 0.525. FunSearch 0.842, above classical on over half of instances. Best agents valid-solution rate 0.555 vs solver 0.611. Search saturates around 50 steps; agents beat classical within about 10 steps.
limits: Figure text extracted with scrambled columns, so per-model scores beyond the ones named are approximate. Normalised scores; o3-mini is the agent backbone; 64-step budget.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 and 5: with reasoning models the one-shot gap shrinks but remains. Select-from-many (BestOfN) is a strong simple baseline and complex planners did not reliably beat it. Run BestOfN as the control for the S7 loop.

source: Chen et al. (2026, ICLR) HeuriGym: An Agentic Benchmark for LLM-Crafted Heuristics in Combinatorial Optimization
finding: Nine frontier models propose heuristics, get execution feedback and refine. Even the best reach a Quality-Yield Index of only about 0.6, far below the expert baseline of 1.
numbers: Top models GPT-o4-mini-high and Gemini-2.5-Pro QYI about 0.6; expert baseline 1.0. Domains: computer systems, logistics, biology.
limits: Abstract and intro read; per-problem tables not extracted.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: 2025 reasoning models still sit well below expert-written heuristics on realistic optimisation. The ceiling for LLM search is lower than for expert code.

source: Chen, Cheng, Sun, Ling, Ge (2026) OPT-Engine: Benchmarking the Limits of LLMs in Optimization Modeling via Complexity Scaling
finding: With DeepSeek V3.2 and GPT-5.1, text-only reasoning degrades sharply as problem size grows. A size cliff is still present for 2025-26 models. On TSP the model enumerates tours at small n, then near the cliff switches to nearest-neighbour and cheapest-insertion heuristics and uses fewer tokens, so quality drops. Writing solver code and calling a solver keeps accuracy at scale.
numbers: Ten OR problem classes scaled from LP to MIP; avg@10 accuracy; models DeepSeek-V3.2 and GPT-5.1 plus Qwen3-4B variants. Exact per-size accuracies are in figures, not text.
limits: Problem is formulation and solving, not trade-off judgment. No exact n for the TSP cliff in the text.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: the OPRO-era size cliff has not gone away for frontier models; it moves. Let code do enumeration and scoring when options are many.

source: Huang, Wu, Zhou, Wu, Feng, Cheng, Tan (2024) Exploring the True Potential: Evaluating the Black-box Optimization Capability of LLMs
finding: First systematic test of LLMs as numerical black-box optimisers. They do poorly on pure numbers but work on discrete problems like TSP at small size, and can use text clues such as city names. Authors warn that promising results come from small sizes or optima near special values.
numbers: TSP optimisation gap / failure count: GPT-3.5 TSP-10 0%, TSP-15 6.01%, TSP-20 30.69%, TSP-25 31.20%; GPT-4 TSP-10 0.00%, TSP-15 0.28%, TSP-20 0.88%, TSP-25 3.38%, TSP-30 11.01%; Gemini TSP-10 0%, TSP-15 4.69%, TSP-20 4.21%; LLaMA 35% to 142%. Authors say LLMs lack exploration-exploitation balance and are slow and costly.
limits: 2023-24 models. Independent of the OPRO and LMEA authors.
agent_relevance: Independent replication of the OPRO size trend: gap grows with n and model strength matters (K01, K02). Also a negative-side result for gap 10.

source: LLMize authors (2026) LLMize: A Framework for Large Language Model-Based Numerical Optimization
finding: Open-source OPRO/LMEA-style framework. Authors conclude it is not competitive with classical solvers on simple problems and is useful where constraints and heuristics are hard to formalise. Weaker gemma-3-27b failed to improve TSP-10 reliably under the same budget, gemini-2.5-flash-lite did.
numbers: TSP N=10 only; best tour about 290 on a 100x100 grid with gemini-2.5-flash-lite; convex test hit target in 2-3 steps (about 26 s); no baseline tables.
limits: Four-page demo with no baselines or repeats; weak evidence. Counted only as an author null statement.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 and gap 4: authors themselves report no edge over classical solvers on simple tasks. Evidence is thin; do not weight it.

source: Liu, Fu, Yogatama, Neiswanger (2024) DeLLMa: Decision Making Under Uncertainty with Large Language Models
finding: Directly prompting LLMs on multi-option decisions does worse as the number of actions grows. A staged procedure (enumerate unknown states, forecast, elicit a utility function by pairwise ranking, compute expected utility in code) beats zero-shot, chain of thought and self-consistency, with a larger gap for bigger action sets. It also beats o1-preview zero-shot at similar cost.
numbers: Up to +40% accuracy over competing methods. Agriculture: DeLLMa 73.3% vs o1-preview 33.3%; Stocks: 64.2% vs 35.0% (best setting, per-action sample size 64, overlap 25%). Cost per instance DeLLMa $0.09-0.37 vs o1 $0.21. Utility-ranking agreement with human 65-70% vs inter-annotator 77.5%. State forecasting ablation: GPT-4 55-60%, Claude 3 32-36%, Gemini 1.5 42-48%.
limits: Decision under uncertainty on two datasets (agriculture, stocks). Utility is one scalar, so criteria count is not varied. GPT-4-era backbone.
agent_relevance: Closest hit for gap 1 and gap 6: a staged, code-aggregated selection beats an LLM picking in one pass at about equal cost, and the benefit grows with option count. Supports S7 as 'LLM scores or ranks pairs, code aggregates'.

source: Shi et al. (2025) Judging the Judges: A Systematic Study of Position Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge
finding: 15 LLM judges show position bias in pairwise and list-wise comparison. It depends on judge, candidate and task, and is strongest when the candidate quality gap is small. It is not much driven by prompt length.
numbers: 15 judges, MT-Bench and DevBench, 22 tasks, about 40 solution models, over 150,000 evaluation instances; metrics repetition stability, position consistency, preference fairness.
limits: Measures judges on answer quality, not on multi-criterion trade-offs.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 6: when options are close in quality, which is the hard S7 case, prompt order decides the pick. Shuffle order and aggregate several passes in code.

source: Xu et al. (2025) Investigating Non-Transitivity in LLM-as-a-Judge
finding: LLM judges give non-transitive preferences (A beats B, B beats C, C beats A), so rankings depend on the baseline model. Non-transitive cases rise sharply as compared items get closer in quality. Round-robin plus Bradley-Terry fixes most of it.
numbers: Spearman with Chatbot Arena 95.0% to 96.4%, Kendall 82.1% to 86.3% with round-robin plus Bradley-Terry. Non-transitive share in the figure runs from about 2.6% to about 40% (figure labels 2.64, 8.91, 27.29, 40.21, bins read from the chart, not the text). SWIM matches round-robin at lower cost.
limits: AlpacaEval instruction following, not engineering trade-offs. Bin definitions not confirmed from text.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: pairwise LLM selection among near-equal candidates is inconsistent. In S7 use a code-side tournament or score aggregation, not a chain of single pairwise picks.

source: Kohli (2026) Nine Judges, Two Effective Votes: Correlated Errors Undermine LLM Evaluation Panels
finding: A panel of 9 frontier LLM judges from 7 families carries only about 2 independent votes of information, because they make the same mistakes. The best single judge matches or beats the panel.
numbers: 3 NLI datasets, 100 human annotations per item. MNLI panel 72.0% vs best judge Qwen3-32B 71.8% (+0.2 pp). About three quarters of nominal independence lost.
limits: NLI labels, not design selection.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: more judge calls from similar models add little. Independent evidence (a code check, different information) is what helps.

source: Kumar, Karniadakis (2026) Agentic Risk-Aware Set-Based Engineering Design
finding: Multi-agent LLM set-based design on airfoil design with a human manager. Tools compute utility and CVaR risk; LLM agents run staged pruning from a large Latin-hypercube set to a short final list, with a human final choice. No comparison with a non-LLM search is reported.
numbers: Stage 2 keeps the top 100 designs by scalar utility (threshold 0.4 equals the RAE2822 benchmark); stage 4 CVaR filter leaves 64 designs; stage 5 keeps top 50; then a rule-based valid/invalid split and CFD on the final set. 9 CST parameters.
limits: Demonstration on one problem, no baseline or ablation, so no evidence the LLM is needed. Not a human study.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 (machine side only): a set-based pipeline where code scores and filters and the LLM proposes and explains. A template for S7 as staged narrowing, with no measured benefit yet.

source: Guo et al. (2025) Toward Engineering AGI: Benchmarking the Engineering Design Capabilities of LLMs (EngDesign)
finding: Engineering design tasks across 9 areas with simulator-based grading. No model passes more than 35% overall, and analog IC design is 0% for all.
numbers: o3 34.38% pass rate, o3-high 33.57%; GPT-4o and Gemini-2.0-Flash about 15%; reasoning models (o3, o4-mini, DeepSeek-R1) beat general chat models; 3 trials per task.
limits: Single-shot with limited iterative refinement; grader-dependent.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: frontier reasoning models still fail most real design tasks. Simulator-graded benchmarks give a measurable target for an S7 test.

source: Deb, Pratap, Agarwal, Meyarivan (2002) A fast and elitist multiobjective genetic algorithm: NSGA-II (re-opened from a UGR course mirror)
finding: Text re-read. Convergence: NSGA-II (real or binary) converges better on all test problems except ZDT3 and ZDT6, where PAES is better; the paper counts this as PAES better on 2 of 9. Diversity: NSGA-II best on all nine. A later passage says SPEA found the best-converged set on ZDT6, so the paper is slightly inconsistent on ZDT6. Fast non-dominated sort is O(MN^2). The constraint rule needs no penalty parameter. One constrained problem (WATER) has five objectives; no systematic many-objective test is reported.
numbers: Population 100, 25,000 function evaluations, 10 runs for PAES, SPEA and NSGA-II; constrained tests used population 100 and 500 generations. NSGA-II parameters were not tuned ('have not made any effort in finding the best parameter setting'); PAES and SPEA used the developers' settings.
limits: Deb's 2001 book still not opened. The many-objective limit (more than 3 objectives) is later work (Ishibuchi et al. 2008, not opened).
agent_relevance: Closes gap 7 for the 2002 paper. Convergence and diversity are separate metrics. NSGA-II was left untuned against rivals, the reverse of the weak-baseline issue.

source: Zhang, Ma, Xu, Xiong, Cheng (2026) Lumina: LLM-guided GPU architecture exploration (re-read for baselines and rules)
finding: Re-read for gaps 2 and 3. Baselines ACO, GA, BO, grid search and random walker ran over 1,000 samples with multiple trials. Random walker and ACO were comparable, BO ranked fourth and stable, GA and grid search failed. LLM accuracy on design tasks is low without human-written corrective rules and rises with them.
numbers: Accuracy original to enhanced (with rules): bottleneck analysis Phi-4 0.70 to 0.76, Qwen-3 0.73 to 0.80, Llama-3.1 0.47 to 0.53; perf/area prediction 0.42 to 0.61, 0.59 to 0.82, 0.23 to 0.39; parameter tuning (trade-off choice under constraints) 0.30 to 0.48, 0.40 to 0.63, 0.26 to 0.46. Benchmark 308, 127 and 30 questions. Lumina beats others by 32.9% PHV and 17.5x sample efficiency.
limits: Baselines look default-style; no tuning described. Rules were written by the authors after seeing failures on the same benchmark, so the lift is partly fit to the test. No rules-only, no-LLM baseline.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partly: rules add 0.12 to 0.23 absolute on trade-off questions, but the rules-only control is missing. Gap 6: unaided trade-off accuracy of 0.26 to 0.40 is low; use rules or code checks.

source: Li, Xiong, Wang (2025) iDSE (re-read for warm-start table and baseline fairness)
finding: All baselines (NSGA-II, ACO, MOEA/D, Lattice, HGBO-DSE) were run in the same rule-pruned design space, so rule pruning is not the source of the 5.1-16.6x lead. The remaining lead comes from LLM warm start and refinement. Warm start is not uniformly best: on autocorr it was much worse than random start.
numbers: Table 3 ADRS ratio to random start (geo mean): NSGA-II BS 1.65x, LHS 1.37x, LLM warm start 3.17x (about 2.3x over LHS); MOEA/D BS 1.97x, LHS 3.14x, warm start 3.41x. autocorr NSGA-II ADRS: random 0.0883, warm start 0.7458 (worse; lower is better). Ablation: baseline LLM invalid designs 12.4%; pruning removes 89.9% of them; reflection +20.5%; domain knowledge +45.0%. Backends tested: DeepSeek-R1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-4.1, Grok-3, o1-preview (figures only, no numbers).
limits: Author-run; baseline parameters not tuned per benchmark. The autocorr exception might relate to diversity loss, but the paper does not test that.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2, 3, 9: baselines were fair on rule pruning, but no non-LLM rule-based seeding is compared. Corrects K10: warm start is 3.17x (NSGA-II) over random start, 2.3x over LHS, not 2.5x.

source: Liu et al. (2024) LLAMBO diversity of warm-start and candidate points (re-read)
finding: LLM warm-start points are more correlated across hyperparameters, so their generalised variance is lower than random start. Direct conditioning on a desired target value gives high-quality candidates but lower diversity; an exploration parameter trades the two.
numbers: Metric: generalised variance (determinant of covariance). LLAMBO spread similar to TPE (Multi), lower than TPE (Ind). Log-likelihood of LLAMBO points highest. Authors note LLM inference costs much more compute than traditional BO; only low-dimensional HPT tasks tested.
limits: No test of whether lower warm-start diversity reduces final regret or Pareto spread; GPT-3.5 backbone.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 stays open: diversity loss is measured, but the effect on final spread is not measured in any paper found.
